title: The lamp and the jewel
hookLine: two glows through two doorways: a lamp and a jewel
carry: meditation on brahman can ripen into knowing
tomorrow: a whole show, and nobody watches the lamp. why not?

cards: Some people won't start until they're sure: the right plan, the right major, the right words. Others start first and figure it out on the way.
Inside Advaita, the same split shows up about meditation, and the Panchadashi answers with two doorways. In one room a lamp is burning. In the other, a jewel shines by its own light.
Two people stand outside. Each sees a soft glow, and each thinks: a jewel. Both run in.
Both were wrong about what they saw. Only one walks out rich.

teach.h: AN ERROR THAT AGREES WITH THE TRUTH.
teach.b: It's the one at the jewel's door. Same mistake, different glow. The book calls it an error that agrees with the truth, and it settles a real disagreement.
One view, held firmly in Advaita: freedom comes only from knowing the self directly. Picturing Brahman, dwelling on a form or a quality like bliss or light, isn't that knowing.
At its best, this view protects people from mistaking a pleasant state for the goal, and from spending a life polishing what was only ever a door.

teach.h: THE OTHER: THE GLOW LEADS IN.
teach.b: The other view, the one this chapter, the lamp of meditation, takes: meditation is chasing the glow of the real jewel. You may not see clearly what you're running toward, but you're running toward the right room.
Steady, long meditation, the book says, can ripen into knowledge itself. Notice the Panchadashi doesn't throw out the first view. It agrees the glow isn't the gem.
It simply won't scorn the person running toward it.
So both voices stay at the table.

teach.h: THE GLOW LEADS TO THE JEWEL.
teach.b: One says: don't confuse the glow with the jewel. The other answers: but the glow is coming from the jewel.

how: In Advaita circles, meditation on a form of God or on a name is commonly kept alongside study, with the teaching that it can ripen into knowledge.

o: a book of Advaita verses that teaches through pictures and stories
a guide to building temples and setting up their images
a book of prayers chanted at weddings and at funerals

p: a mistake that finds the jewel
walking all the way into the room

s: the Panchadashi scorns people who meditate on a form of God
it says their practice follows the glow of the real jewel.
the book calls meditation an error that agrees with the truth
same mistake as the lamp-chaser, but it was the glow of the real thing.
in Advaita, meditation and knowing the self are the same thing
the glow isn't the gem; meditation can ripen into knowledge.

games.q: you side with the Panchadashi: meditation can ripen into knowledge. a friend holds the strict view. say that view's best case.
o: it guards against mistaking a calm state for the goal itself.
it says meditation is useless and nobody should do it.
it says knowledge comes from reading, never from sitting.
games.why: the strict view's strength is a warning: the glow isn't the gem. the Panchadashi agrees, and still honors the one running toward it.

practice: Choose one short word to say softly aloud on each out-breath: a name of God if you pray, the sound om, or a plain word like peace. Keep it slow and unhurried.
When the mind wanders, come back to the same word, the way someone keeps walking toward the same glow.

wordCard.voice: The Panchadashi: today, the book that calls meditation a mistake worth making, because it follows the glow of the real jewel.

orig.note: Sanskrit: meditation; the chapter is the Dhyanadipa, the lamp of meditation.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: meditation on Brahman can ripen into knowing. The glow of the real jewel leads to the jewel.

sources.ref: Panchadashi 9 (Dhyanadipa): the light of a gem and the light of a lamp, both mistaken for a gem; the one who goes to the gem's light gets the gem (samvadi bhrama, an error that agrees with the truth); meditation on Brahman can lead to knowledge
